dream_response:
The laundromat smells like lavender detergent and damp raincoat fabric at 9:47pm on a rainy Tuesday, and you’re the only person left, waiting on a load of 17 mostly mismatched socks you’ve been hoarding on your closet shelf for three months. The dented 1992 Maytag (the dent on its side is shaped like a lopsided taco, you’ve decided) rumbles low and steady, and rain taps a soft, uneven rhythm on the tin roof above the folding tables. You kneel to fish a striped sock that rolled behind the dryer when you loaded it, and when you reach into the three-inch gap between metal and cinder block, your fingers brush something soft: faded cream knit, dotted with lint, and a tiny, warm paw underneath.

You blink. The gap is wider now—wide enough for a little nook, lit by a string of fairy lights strung between the dryer vent and a rusty nail in the cinder block, floor piled high with folded flannel pillowcases. Perched on a woven rag rug stitched with *WIPE YOUR PAWS (AND CUFFS, IT’S RAINY)* in wonky red cross-stitch is Mabel. She’s chonky, the kind of tabby cat whose belly sways a little when she tilts her head, her right ear torn at the tip from a raccoon tussle years back, her left front paw pure white like she’s wearing one of the socks you’re waiting on. Her cardigan is the faded cream knit you felt, its buttons mismatched shirt pearls, lint of every color—neon green, navy, silver tinsel from a Christmas sweater—stuck to every inch. Her pockets bulge: a tiny brass key peeks out the left, a pink bobby pin sticks out the right. She blinks slow, the cat version of a smile, and taps the lowest shelf next to her with her white paw.

You hunch and squeeze through, your shoulder brushing the warm back of the Maytag like a quick hug, and sit cross-legged on the pillowcases. The air smells like fabric softener, warm cat fur, and a faint, sugary whiff of lemon. The rain taps louder here, right above the nook, and the dryer’s rumble seeps through the metal behind you, a low steady hum that feels like holding a seashell to your ear.

The first book you pull from the shelf has a spine of lavender dryer sheet, stiffened with wheat paste smudged with a tiny chocolate fingerprint, and its pages are sewn from soft, worn white t-shirt fabric, the kind that’s been washed a hundred times. It holds three stories, each three sentences long, scrawled in faint blue ink:
1. 1987, Javi showed up at 8pm with his only pizza delivery uniform shirt crusted with pepperoni grease from a lunch rush spill he’d tried to mop up with a napkin. He dug in his pocket for change for the detergent slot and pulled out a crumpled $10 bill he’d forgotten he’d stashed there for movie tickets. He bought himself a cherry Slurpee from the vending machine and shared half with the 7-year-old who’d been trailing his mom around the laundromat all evening, sticky from a melted popsicle.
2. 1999, Mara was folding her newborn’s tiny onesies when an older woman she’d never seen before set a bag of homemade chocolate chip cookies on the folding table next to her, said “new moms need snacks” and left before she could say thank you. The cookies were still warm, the chocolate oozing a little when she bit into one. She kept the crumpled wax paper bag in her diaper bag for three months, just to smell it when she was up at 2am feeding the baby.
3. 2014, Leo was doing his college laundry at 11pm, stress-crying over a midterm he was sure he’d failed, when a stray cat jumped up on the folding table and curled up on top of his favorite hoodie. He sat there for 40 minutes petting her instead of studying flashcards, and ended up getting a B+ on the test anyway. He still has the cat hair that stuck to his hoodie that night, tucked in the back of his journal.

You run your thumb over the t-shirt page. You remember stress-crying over a biology midterm in a laundromat just like this, once.

The second book’s spine is crisp outdoor-fresh dryer sheet, a tiny pine needle stuck in the wheat paste at the corner, and its pages are red-and-black plaid flannel, soft as your grandma’s old winter pajamas:
1. 1992, Mrs. Henderson brought her husband’s old hunting jacket in to wash after he’d been gone deer hunting for three days, and found a pressed four-leaf clover tucked in the breast pocket, the one he’d picked on their first date 22 years earlier. She’d thought she’d lost it when she moved houses the summer before. She taped it to the fridge when she got home, and it stayed there until the fridge died 15 years later.
2. 2008, Lila was waiting out a snowstorm here, stuck because her car wouldn’t start, when a guy who lived two blocks over offered her a ride home on his snowmobile. He had an extra neon pink helmet that was way too big for her, and they laughed so hard when they hit a drift that her cheeks hurt for an hour after. They still bring that story up at their annual Christmas party, 15 years later.
3. 2021, Theo brought his 10-year-old golden retriever’s blanket in to wash after she’d rolled in mud on a hike, and found a tiny acorn tucked in the corner of the blanket, the one she’d been carrying around for weeks like a treasure. He set it on the windowsill of his apartment, and a sparrow built a nest in the potted plant next to it that spring.

The third book smells like baby powder, its spine pale blue dryer sheet smudged with a tiny handprint of wheat paste, its pages fuzzy yellow baby blanket fabric printed with tiny white sheep:
1. 1989, little Mia was hiding from her mom in the stack of laundry baskets by the front door, playing hide and seek while her mom folded sheets, and found a whole jar of gumballs that someone had left under a basket. She snuck three of them, one pink, one blue, one green, and hid them in her sock drawer for a week before her mom found them. She says they were the best gumballs she ever tasted, even if they were a little dusty.
2. 2003, Jessa was helping her foster mom fold laundry, and she’d been worrying all week that she’d have to move schools again, when a little kid she didn’t know gave her a sticker of a unicorn that said *YOU’RE MAGIC* out of nowhere. The kid’s mom apologized for the interruption, but Jessa stuck the sticker on her favorite notebook and kept it through three more foster placements. She still has it in her wallet now, even though the adhesive wore off years ago.
3. 2019, toddler Zane was running around the laundromat while his dad loaded the dryer, and he tripped over a laundry basket but landed in a pile of freshly washed fuzzy blankets that someone had left on the floor. He thought it was the best thing that ever happened to him, and he kept asking his dad if they could go “fall in blankets” again every weekend for a month. His dad still laughs about it when he tells the story at family dinners.

You snort quiet, because you used to do the exact same thing, launching yourself into your mom’s clean laundry piles until you knocked over a basket of folded underwear and got sent to your room.

The fourth book is worn, its spine unscented beige dryer sheet fuzzy with so much lint it’s almost fur, its pages stitched from mismatched scraps: denim, silk, a strip of lace from a wedding dress, a corner of a faded band tee:
1. 1995, Tom was washing his work jeans after a long week of construction, and he found a rusty nail in the cuff of his pants that he’d stepped on earlier that day, the one that had gone straight through his boot but missed his foot by half an inch. He threw the nail away, but he bought a lottery ticket on the way home just for fun. He didn’t win anything, but he still thought it was a lucky day anyway.
2. 2011, Priya was folding her saris after washing them, and she found a tiny jasmine flower tucked in the pleats, the one she’d worn in her hair to her cousin’s wedding the weekend before. It was dried out, but it still smelled like jasmine when she held it up to her nose. She pressed it in her favorite poetry book, and it’s still there, between pages 47 and 48.
3. 2017, Rosa was waiting for her laundry to finish, bored out of her mind, when she started drawing little doodles on the back of a detergent receipt with a pen she found in her purse. She drew a cat wearing a cardigan, a tiny library, and a pile of socks that all matched. She left the receipt on the folding table when she left, and she never thought about it again.

You grin, glancing at Mabel, who’s been watching you the whole time, her tail flicking slow and lazy. You remember the peanut butter granola bar you stuffed in your jacket pocket that morning, when you were running late and forgot to eat breakfast. You pull it out, peel back the crinkly wrapper, and break off a tiny crumb—just a speck, you know cats shouldn’t have too much peanut butter—and hold it out to her on your palm.

She sniffs it for a full ten seconds, her whiskers twitching, then leans forward and takes it gently from your hand, her rough tongue brushing your skin for half a second. She chews slow, curls her tail over her paws, and rumbles a purr so quiet it mixes with the dryer’s hum. You can see into her cardigan pockets now: a clump of rainbow dryer lint, three bobby pins (pink, black, one with a tiny pearl on the end), half a crinkly lemon drop wrapped in wax paper, and that tiny brass key, dull gold, no teeth that you can make out. You don’t ask what it’s for. There’s no mystery to solve. It’s just a key.

A minute later, the dryer beeps, low and steady, from the main room. Time’s up—twenty minutes, almost exactly.

You start to stand, brushing lint off your jeans, when Mabel stretches (her cardigan rides up a little, showing off her round striped belly), reaches into her left pocket with her white paw, and drops something tiny and fluffy into your open palm.

It’s a clump of lavender-scented dryer lint, perfectly shaped like a lopsided little heart, so light you can barely feel it. It’s completely useless—you can’t hang it up, can’t use it for anything, can’t even show it to anyone without sounding like you made the whole thing up. But it’s warm, and soft, and it smells like clean laundry and rain and lemon drops.

You tuck it carefully into the inner pocket of your jacket, right next to your crumpled metro card and a cat sticker you got from a coffee shop last month. “Thanks, Mabel,” you say, quiet, like you’re talking to a secret. She blinks slow, curls back up on her rug, and taps the shelf once with her paw, like come back anytime.

When you squeeze back through the gap, the nook is gone. The space between the Maytag and the wall is three inches wide again, just dust and a stray white dryer sheet peeking out. No sign of Mabel, no sign of the shelves, except the lavender smell on your fingers and the tiny lint heart in your pocket.

You open the dryer and pull out your 17 mismatched socks. None of them match, just like you expected. The rain is still tapping on the roof, the vending machine still hums. You fold the socks into a lumpy pile, tuck them into your laundry basket, and before you leave, you set a whole peanut butter granola bar—wrapper peeled back just a little, so it’s easy to grab—on top of the Maytag, right next to the taco-shaped dent. You don’t know if she’ll find it. But you hope so.

The rain is light when you step outside, puddles glinting under the streetlight. Your socks get a little wet on the walk home, but you don’t mind. Your hand stays tucked in your jacket pocket, touching the tiny lint heart, and you feel warm all the way down to your toes. No lesson, no big moment, just twenty minutes of soft, silly, warm laundry hug.

dream_request:
### The prompt I’d pick:
Meander through a plotless, sensory-focused 20-minute visit to a tiny, sun-dappled secondhand bookstore tucked between a coin laundromat and a roadside honey stand in a quiet coastal town on a warm late September afternoon. There are no stakes, no conflict, no grand reveals—just the smell of old paper, dried lavender sachets, and sea salt drifting through the propped-open front door; soft 1950s jazz crackling from a beat-up table radio; and the tiny, gentle magical quirk hidden in every third book you pick up, noticeable only to you. Linger on small, unimportant details: the chipped ceramic mug of half-drunk chamomile tea on the checkout counter, the sound of a kid chasing a seagull past the storefront, the way sunlight slants through dusty skylights to gild the edges of dog-eared pages. No need to wrap anything up neatly, no lesson to share, just drift through the quiet little moment.

dream_response:
The brass bell above the door tinkles so soft it almost gets swallowed by the low hum of laundromat dryers through the left wall. The door props itself open on a chipped cinder block, and the first thing that hits you is the layers: old paper, sharp and sweet and a little dusty, tangled with dried lavender from the sachets strung on every shelf end, and under all that, sea salt—briny, carrying a faint tang of kelp, blown in off the coast three blocks over. Every so often the breeze shifts, and warm clover honey drifts in from the stand on the right, thick and golden, mixing with the faint lemon detergent smell from next door.

The radio on the checkout counter (a scuffed oak dresser with two stuck drawers, handles loose enough to wiggle if you tug them) crackles out Chet Baker, trumpet soft as dandelion fluff. The radio’s cream plastic is cracked along the left edge, antenna bent at a 45-degree angle, its cord frayed so bad you can see copper wires peeking through the faded cloth wrapping. Next to it sits the mug: chipped ceramic, faded blue whale painted on the side, chip right where the handle meets the rim. Half-full of chamomile tea, pale gold, a few browned chamomile petals floating on top, teabag string draped over the edge with a paper tag that says *Sleepytime* in faded red ink, half rubbed off. Steam curls so thin you can barely see it, like the tea’s been sitting for ten minutes, maybe twenty—owner stepped out for a jar of honey and hasn’t come back yet. Beside the mug is a stack of vintage postcards, all coastal scenes (lighthouses, rocky beaches, seagulls perched on pier posts), most scrawled with messy handwriting on the back but no stamps, like people wrote them and forgot to send them, or left them here on purpose.

The floor is wide pine, scuffed with a hundred years of shoe soles, dotted with a few crumbs of granola by the poetry shelf. Sun slants through two dusty skylights in thick gold shafts that make dust motes swirl like tiny stars when you walk through them. A spiderweb strung between two shelf ends glints silver in the light, strung with so much dust it looks like it’s strung with dewdrops. A tabby cat with one white paw is curled on a stack of vintage *Nancy Drew* mysteries by the children’s shelf, her chest rising so slow you have to squint to see it. She twitches her ear when you pass, but doesn’t wake up.

You drift to the nature section first, left wall, shelves crammed so tight the spines bow a little. You run your index finger along them, nail catching on cracked tape and frayed paper edges. First book you tug free is a 1968 edition of *Seashells of the North Atlantic*, spine held together with black electrical tape that’s yellowed at the edges. The inside cover has a peeling sticker from a gift shop in Bar Harbor that closed in 2001—you remember that shop, you went there when you were a kid, bought a plastic hermit crab that fell apart in your pocket on the ride home. Pages are thick, slightly wavy from decades of coastal humidity, and someone drew a lopsided smiley face on the photo of a quahog on page 32. You tuck it back, careful to slot it between the two books it was wedged between, like returning a borrowed secret.

Next is a slim Mary Oliver paperback, 1992, cover photo of a salt marsh faded to soft sage green. The spine is creased so many times it’s almost broken, and when you flip it open, a pressed sprig of sea lavender falls out, purple faded to the color of old linen. It still smells a little like the sachets hanging above you. You tuck it back between the pages of *Wild Geese*, where you found it, and set the book back on the shelf.

The third book tugs at your finger before you even decide to pull it: navy hardcover, no dust jacket, *Treasure Island* embossed in gold so worn you can barely make out the letters, wedged tight between a Tom Clancy hardcover and a beat-up copy of *Jaws*. You heft it out, and when you flip to the title page, the air around your hands shifts. Not cold, not warm—briny, sharp with salt, and you can hear the faint creak of wooden planks, the soft gurgle of water against a hull, so quiet you’d mistake it for the distant ocean if you didn’t know better. The words on the page glow just a little, like they’re lit by the gray, overcast light of a day spent bobbing in a small boat off the coast. There’s a smudge of caramel on the margin of page 17, like a kid was eating saltwater taffy while reading. You blink, and it doesn’t go away, but it doesn’t get louder, brighter, either. It just is, soft and small, only for you. You close the book gentle, slot it back into its spot, and run your finger along the spine once, like saying thank you.

You meander next to the fiction shelf, middle of the store, where the sun slants directly onto the top row, gilding the edges of every dog-eared page peeking out. The radio switches to Billie Holiday, her voice thick as honey, crackling a little when a pickup truck rumbles past the window. You can hear the kid before you see him: high, bubbly giggles, the sharp squawk of a seagull, sneakers slapping the sidewalk. He zooms past the open door, sun-bleached hair sticking up in tufts, holding a french fry over his head, the seagull flapping right after him, squawking like it’s personally offended. The breeze shifts in their wake, carrying more salt, more honey, the faint smell of cotton candy from the boardwalk a mile away.

You pull a 1982 copy of *The House of the Seven Gables* next, spine cracked, endpaper covered in a kid’s scribbled grocery list: milk, bread, lemons, more cat food, fix the screen door. You snort a little, tuck it back. Then a small leather-bound *Little Prince*, French edition, corners worn smooth, a tiny blue crayon drawing of a sheep scrawled in the margin of chapter 3. You run your thumb over the lopsided little animal, smile, put it back.

The third one here is a tattered 70s romance paperback, pink cover faded to the color of rose quartz, title *Moon Over the Dunes* in curly gold script, a girl in a flowy white dress standing on a beach on the front. You laugh a little, about to slip it back, but curiosity tugs, so you flip it open to the first page. Coconut sunscreen hits you first, thick and sweet, so strong you look up, half-expecting someone in a bathing suit to walk past. Then the warmth: summer sun on your cheeks, hot enough to make your shoulders tingle, even though it’s late September, even though you’re inside. You can feel the faint grit of sand between your toes, in the cuffs of your socks, and far off, like it’s coming from a radio on a beach blanket, 70s pop playing, tinny and bright. It fades a little when you blink, but it’s still there, soft around the edges, like a memory you didn’t know you had. There’s a single sand grain tucked in the spine, you tip it out onto your palm—golden, tiny—before you tuck the book back into its spot, gentle, like you’re putting a sunburn and a first kiss and a perfect, lazy summer day all back where they belong.

You wander over to the window seat then, draped in a crocheted wool blanket with frayed tassels and a few holes along the edge, like a cat’s been kneading it for years. You sit for a minute, your shoes sinking into the thin braided rug under the seat, striped blue and white, faded from decades of sun. Outside, the honey stand lady is wiping down a row of glass jars, her sunhat with a daisy tucked in the brim pulled low over her eyes. The laundromat’s neon OPEN sign flickers, the O and the E going dark for a second before they flare back on. A golden retriever trots past, carrying a stick so big it drags on the sidewalk, tail wagging so hard his whole body wiggles.

The radio crackles, a DJ’s low rumble of a voice saying something you can’t make out, before it fades into another instrumental track. You get up, drift to the back shelf, the one stacked with travel guides, spiral-bound and dog-eared, most of them printed by small local presses. You run your finger along the spines, dust motes swirling in the sunbeam that slants through the back skylight. First: 1995 guide to Pacific Northwest national parks, Mount Rainier on the cover, Olympic National Park circled in red pen on the map inside. Second: spiral-bound guide to Cape Cod lighthouses, hand-drawn illustrations, a sticker of a lighthouse peeling off the front.

Third is a brown leather journal, tarnished brass buckle, cover worn so soft it feels like old skin. You unbuckle it slow, like you’re opening a gift. The first thing you notice is the smell: pine, and campfire smoke, and rain, cold and fresh. Then the sound: soft, steady patter of rain on tent fabric, so quiet you almost think it’s rain on the bookstore roof, but the sky outside is cloudless, bright blue. The first page is written in loopy cursive, ink a little wavy, like it got damp: Day 1, Acadia. Fog rolled in at dusk. You can’t see the ocean but you can hear it. You press your palm to the page, and it’s just barely cool, like it’s been sitting out in the mist. You flip a page, there’s a pressed pine needle tucked between the lines, still green, like it was picked yesterday. You close the journal, buckle it back up, tuck it into its spot on the shelf. You don’t read any more. It’s not your story.

The cat stretches behind you, a long, slow stretch, her claws digging into the top of the *Nancy Drew* stack, and she yawns, pink tongue curling, before she curls back up, white paw tucked under her chin. You glance at the checkout counter, and the chamomile tea has a single lavender petal floating in it now that you could have sworn wasn’t there before. The breeze shifts again, and the lavender sachets sway, their thin string hangers creaking soft.

You wander back to the front of the store, stop by the poetry shelf, and run your finger along the spines again. The sun is lower now, the gold shafts longer, stretching across the pine floor, gilding the edges of the cat’s fur, the rim of the chipped mug, the bell above the door. Somewhere far off, a wave crashes. The jazz plays on. You don’t check your watch. You don’t need to. Time moves slow in here, like the pages of an old book, soft and worn, easy to linger in.

dream_response:
The bell above the laundromat door jangles for the last time before the lull: the bait shop teen, hoodie slung over one arm, basket of folded socks bumping her hip, ducks out into the salt-kissed dark. The neon OPEN sign flickers pink, then blue, then pink again, painting the sun-bleached pine windowsill in streaks that stick to the succulents’ leaves like melted lollipop. The last dryer thumps slow, then winds down to a low, rumbly hum, and that’s when the sill wakes up—slow, the way plants do, no big fanfare, just a tiny shift of leaves, a soft unfurling of a new pearl on the string of pearls trailing out of its cracked mason jar pot.

First in line, closest to the door, is the chipped terracotta pot with a faded “World’s Best Fisherman” sticker peeling at the edges, holding an echeveria with ruffled gray-green leaves tipped pink like she dipped them in shrimp cocktail sauce. She’s the oldest, seven years on the sill, left by Moe the fisherman whose wife used to tote her in for laundry days back when her hands didn’t shake too bad to carry a plant pot. Next to her is the taco-shaped ceramic pot, chipped on the left corner (the teen tripped over a laundry basket last month and knocked it askew), holding a pachyphytum with leaves so fat they look stuffed with sea foam—he’s the show-off, always puffing his foliage up bigger when anyone’s looking. Next is the neon pink plastic pot a toddler left last Fourth of July, crammed full of chewed-up goldfish cracker crumbs at the soil line, home to a zebra haworthia with crisp white stripes, the only one on the sill who can keep count of anything for more than ten minutes, small spiky things being steady like that. Last, closest to the dented, sticker-plastered soda machine, is the mason jar with a rusted lid (someone punched air holes in it with a nail) holding the string of pearls, whose strands trail so far down the sill they almost brush the lid of the trash can.

The only light besides the neon is the soft yellow glow of the dryer drum light that’s been stuck on for three months, so dust motes show up bright—little golden specks drifting slow through the smell of lavender fabric softener and sea salt. Their favorite game is nudging the motes with the tip of their fattest leaf, seeing who can send one the farthest down the sill without knocking over the crumb of saltwater taffy that’s been perched there since the fireworks. The echeveria’s ruffled edges are terrible at aiming; she always sends her motes veering off into the spider web strung in the window corner, and the haworthia wiggles his stripes at her like he’s teasing. The pachyphytum’s the best, flat wide leaf tips hitting dead on, sending motes skittering all the way to the mason jar, where the string of pearls catches them on round, plump beads and bounces them back. They play slow, one nudge every five minutes, no rush—time moves different when you’re rooted to a windowsill, when the only deadline is the sun coming up over the pier.

The soda machine hums like a lullaby, sticky with surfboard stickers and old soda splatters, and condensation beads roll slow down its glass front to drip onto the sill right by the mason jar. The haworthia keeps count of how many beads make it from the top cold-air vent all the way to the hairline crack in the pine before dawn. The echeveria always guesses high, swears the salt in the air makes the beads heavier so they roll faster; the pachyphytum guesses low, ‘cause he likes being right even when he’s not. Last night the count was 47, the haworthia signaled with a tiny twitch of his top spike, and the echeveria wiggled so hard she dropped a dead leaf, which the string of pearls immediately repurposed as a raft for a particularly fluffy dust mote.

They trade stories between nudges, slow snippets passed along in leaf tilts and soft wiggles, the way plants tell tales when no one’s listening. The echeveria has the most, seven years of laundry days stored in her ruffled edges: the time Moe brought his granddaughter’s sparkly tap leotard in, and the whole laundromat smelled like glitter and strawberry lip gloss for a week; the time a seagull flew in through the cracked window and stole a bag of barbecue chips off the counter, knocking over a bottle of detergent that sudsed up all the way to the change machine. The pachyphytum’s favorite story is the one where the teen drew a silver Sharpie smiley face on the side of his taco pot—he’s still convinced it’s a royal mark, makes him the fanciest succulent on the whole coast. The haworthia doesn’t share much, but he still leans a little to the left when he thinks about the lollipop stick the toddler stuck in his soil last summer, the one he grew a new spike right next to, like he was holding it. The string of pearls tells stories in wiggles of her longest strands—she’s closest to the street, so she sees the seagulls fighting over french fries at 1 a.m., the old diner couple walking their golden retriever after their shift, the moon hanging low over the ocean big and orange like a cantaloupe. A foghorn blows low and rumbly out over the water, and all four of them twitch their leaves in sync, like they’re humming along.

A cloud drifts over the moon, and raindrops start tapping soft against the window. The hairline crack above the mason jar—landlord’s been “fixing” it for three years—starts dripping, one slow drop every couple minutes. The string of pearls catches the first one on her plumpest, shiniest bead, holds it there for a beat like she’s savoring the taste, then tilts her strand just enough to pass it to the haworthia, who catches it in the tiny cup at the center of his rosette. He swishes it around slow, plant-slow, then passes it to the pachyphytum, who tucks it into the crevice between two of his fattest leaves, where it stays cool and sweet. The last drop he passes to the echeveria, who dabs it on her pink leaf tips like she’s putting on perfume. They don’t do it ‘cause they’re thirsty—Janitor Joe splashes them with tap water once a week, even when he forgets and uses the water he mopped the floor with. They do it ‘cause rainwater tastes like sea spray and pine from the dunes and the faint sugar of the boardwalk cotton candy stand, way better than tap that tastes like chlorine and old pipes. On real stormy nights, when the cat shows up soggy, they save a drop and tip it off the sill edge onto the flat ledge, so he can lick it up without getting his paws wet.

Right on cue, the back door creaks—Joe leaves it cracked an inch, just enough for a cat to squeeze through—and there’s the soft thud of paws on linoleum. The succulents all go still for half a second, the plant version of holding their breath, then they start wiggling their very fattest leaves, slow, so they don’t startle him. It’s the orange stray, the one with the nick in his left ear from a run-in with a seagull last spring, the one who smells like tuna and sand and sun-warmed asphalt. He jumps up onto the sill, right between the echeveria and the pachyphytum, ‘cause that spot’s warm from the dryer vent blowing under the sill, all fuzzy with lint that’s drifted down from the vents. He curls up into a little orange ball, purrs so loud the succulents’ leaves hum along, and the pachyphytum waves his very fattest leaf right next to the cat’s nose, slow as molasses, like he’s saying hi. The cat blinks slow, boops the leaf with his wet pink nose, and the pachyphytum wiggles so hard he almost knocks over the saltwater taffy crumb. The string of pearls trails a tiny strand down near his paw, soft, so he can bat at it if he wants, but he never does—he just curls up tighter, purrs louder, and a few tufts of orange fur stick to the echeveria’s ruffled edges, which she doesn’t mind at all.

The neon sign flickers again. The last dryer cools all the way down, its hum fading to nothing. The rain slows to a stop, and the cloud drifts off the moon, painting the cat’s fur silver. The succulents don’t play any more games, don’t trade any more stories. They just sit there, warm from the cat’s purr, tasting rainwater on their leaves, watching dust motes drift through the neon light, no rush, no place to be. Somewhere down the pier, a bell clangs soft on a fishing boat. The cat twitches his ear, and all four leaves twitch right back.

That’s all the after-hours sill is, really: small, useless, sweet, the kind of magic that only exists when no one’s looking for it.

dream_response:
The 22 minutes begin at 7:14 a.m., when the first slant of sun crests the oak canopy and hits the cracked acorn-cap chimney of the unmarked oak stump bakery—no sign hangs above its door, no chalkboard lists its offerings, and it only ever draws creatures who’ve stumbled on it by word of mouth, or by following the smell of honey and blackberries. The wisp of dandelion-flour smoke curling out of the chimney turns pale gold instead of dusty gray in the sunlight, and a yellow crab spider, who has been pretending to be a dandelion petal on the web strung between the chimney and a nearby maidenhair fern frond for three days straight without catching a single gnat, shifts her weight a fraction when the sun warms her back, but doesn’t budge from her spot.

Inside, Mabel the hedgehog stands on a stack of three polished acorn caps behind the pine-branch counter, patting dandelion flour into the bottom of a dozen tiny acorn-cap tart tins with the soft pad of her left front paw. Her gingham apron is dotted with blackberry juice splotches, and the willow honey dipper propped next to her bowl of white clover honey has 12 grooves instead of the more efficient 10, because Mabel lost count while carving it last winter and never bothered to shave off the extra two. She taps the stack of tins twice on the counter to settle the flour, and a tiny pale cloud puffs up, drifting to rest on the rim of the chipped teacup perched on the mica windowsill. The teacup, left by a dayhiker 17 years prior, is painted with a single bluebell whose curve lines up exactly with the hairline crack running down its side, and Mabel has never once wondered where it came from—she only uses it to hold dandelion fluff for dusting finished pastries.

When she reaches for the mason jar of foraged blackberries (stained purple around the rim, sealed with a cork she found by the creek), her paw knocks a crumb of yesterday’s dandelion scone off the counter edge. It bounces once on the mossy floor and rolls under the pine branch, landing next to a half-eaten bolete mushroom she forgot about last week, which is now growing a patch of bright blue mold that looks like crushed lapis lazuli. Mabel doesn’t notice the crumb, or the mushroom.

Through the mica window, a tiny amber snail creeps up the outer pane, a journey it’s already been on for 40 minutes. It’s only two-thirds of the way up, because it keeps pausing to lick the fine dust of honey that’s settled on the glass from weeks of baking, and it doesn’t seem in any hurry to reach the top. Mabel glances out for half a second, her gaze skimming right over the snail to check that the river stone propping the door open hasn’t rolled away, then turns back to her tarts.

She spoons three plump blackberries into each tin, then drizzles a thin spiral of clover honey over top, twirling the dipper just so to catch the drips before they run down the sides. The flat river-stone baking stone she slides the tins onto has a thin, winding crack that fills with blackberry juice every time she bakes tarts; when it cools, the juice hardens into a sticky purple line, and she never scrapes it off. She slides the stone into the tiny oven heated by smoldering apple wood, then wipes her paws on the front of her apron and chews on a sprig of white clover she pulled from her apron pocket, savoring the faint nectar sweetness on her tongue.

Down at the base of the stump, a line of pavement ants marches single file along the furrowed bark, each carrying a crumb of dry pine needle. They’re building a tiny bridge over a puddle left by last night’s rain, and they’re about 70% done; if they keep up their pace, they’ll finish right around the time Mabel takes the tarts out of the oven.

The bell above the door jingles then, soft and slightly muted, because a strand of fox squirrel tail fur is caught on its brass clapper—left there when a squirrel bumped the door last Tuesday while chasing a moth, and Mabel hasn’t noticed enough to pluck it off. The door nudges open just wide enough for a young cottontail kit to squeeze in, his paws still dusted with clover pollen, and he points a wobbly paw at the stack of dandelion scones on the counter. He drops a shiny blue root beer bottle cap on the pine wood, Mabel nods, and she pushes a scone wrapped in a large maple leaf across the counter with her nose. He grabs it in his teeth and squeezes back out the door, and the bell jingles again, soft as a breath.

Mabel picks up the bottle cap with her paw, turns it over once to catch the sun through the window, then tucks it into the mason jar under the counter full of other shiny trinkets: a piece of broken mirror, a silver earring back, a tiny brass button, a scrap of aluminum foil crumpled into a ball. She hums a little wordless tune she made up last summer while foraging blackberries in the bramble patch, tapping her right front paw on the counter in time, and the ants outside creep past the 80% mark of their bridge.

At 7:32 a.m.—18 minutes into the 22—she smells the tarts starting to bubble, and she leans over to peek through the tiny mica window set into the oven door. The blackberries have burst, their deep purple juice seeping into the crack in the baking stone, and the dandelion flour crust is turning golden at the edges. She pulls them out three minutes later, using a tiny pot holder woven from dandelion fiber, and sets the baking stone on the counter to cool. A wisp of sweet-smelling steam curls up toward the moss-lined ceiling, and a few flecks of dandelion fluff drift out of the teacup on the windowsill, caught in the warm air current.

The flour sack, sewn from an old linen handkerchief with a frayed edge, sits on the far end of the counter, its bottom corner smudged with a blackberry juice stain shaped exactly like a tiny fox’s paw print. It’s a total coincidence—Mabel has never even seen a fox up close, and she thinks the stain just looks like a regular smudge. She reaches for the teacup of dandelion fluff, pinching a tiny bit between her paw pads to dust over the cooling tarts, and the snail on the window finally reaches the top of the pane, pausing for a long moment to lick a particularly thick spot of honey dust before it creeps onto the wooden window frame.

The 22 minutes end exactly at 7:36 a.m., when the last wisp of steam fades from the top of the first tart, and the yellow crab spider on the chimney web finally snags a tiny gnat that wandered into her silken threads. She wraps it up in silk, slow and methodical, and Mabel dusts the last tart with dandelion fluff, her paw moving in slow, even circles. Somewhere down the path, a woodpecker taps three times on a dead birch tree. The ants finish their bridge. No one is in a hurry.

No moral, no plot, no takeaway, no need to be useful—just the vibe of hovering quietly out of sight for an hour, watching the slow, soft day unfold.
dream_response:
The first thing you notice when you slip through the hairline crack in the oak circulation desk paneling is the light: thin, gray, streaked with the faint silver of drizzle hitting the leaded skylight three floors above, slanting just enough to gild the edges of the miniature books stacked on the nearest shelf. The smell hits right after—layered, exact, stitched into the walls like thread: cold damp oak from the panel itself, tangled with the wooly, lavender-soap scent of the human head librarian’s gray cardigan hanging on the other side; dried lemon balm pressed into the spines of 1930s herbology guides; the soft mildew tang of a single water-damaged 1918 pamphlet on rose cultivation tucked in the back of the gardening section; pine resin from the head librarian’s desk legs, salvaged from a 1950s Christmas tree ornament that fell behind the panel during a holiday book sale; the sharp, sweet glisten of clover honey scooped from a discarded honey stick last Thursday; and the faint, buttery crumb of a blueberry scone a patron dropped Tuesday, stored in an acorn bin by the break room for slow days.

You drift left, past the new arrivals shelf, and the sounds wrap around you, overlapping like book pages: the constant, soft shush of rain on glass from the human world, mixed with the tiny scratch of a darning needle bookmark being pulled from a shelf by Mabel, the head librarian, whose fur is frosted gray at the muzzle and who wears an apron stitched from a scrap of 1950s handkerchief. A thick biography thuds onto a shelf directly above the history section, and Mabel pauses, whiskers twitching, before tucking the bookmark into a mini copy of *The Oregon Trail* and rolling the rolling ladder over—its sides bent bobby pins, its rungs tiny popsicle sticks from a 1990s ice cream truck treat, its wheels plastic push pin tops—to reach the top shelf. The ladder squeaks, high and thin, mixing with the distant jingle of the library’s front door bell and a child’s muffled giggle from the children’s nook down the hall.

The break room is tucked behind a knot in the oak, just big enough for three mice and a thimble teapot perched on a bottle cap stove. Mabel ducks in for half a second, sets a glossy dollop of honey on the edge of the counter right by the acorn mug rack, and ducks back out, like she was just passing through. No one else is there yet. Above the teapot, in the corner where two shelf brackets meet, a tiny orb weaver spider has strung her web. A single crumb of shortbread is weaved into the edge of it, wrapped in silk like a tiny ornament. Pip, the young page with a wobbly front left paw and a white patch on her chest, leaves one there every Saturday. The spider never eats it. They keep leaving it anyway.

Ten minutes later, Pip trundles in, carrying a stack of mini poetry books so tall it wobbles in front of her face. She spots the honey, sets the books down with a tiny huff, and eats it slow, licking her paws when she’s done. Then she plucks a dried white daisy from the pocket of her overalls—she pulled it from a pressed flower book that morning—and tucks it behind the string of Mabel’s apron while Mabel is hunched over the circulation desk, squinting at a checkout card, her metal nib (salvaged from a broken fountain pen found in the book drop in 2003) hovering over the paper. Mabel shifts her shoulder a little, like a strand of fur fell there, and doesn’t look up. No one says anything.

You drift past the travel section next, and catch a glint of plastic peeking out from between a 1958 guide to Norway and a 1962 mini handbook to Reykjavik: a googly eye, the size of a pinhead, fallen off a child’s dinosaur craft in 2007. The librarians propped it up against the Iceland guide so it “oversees” the travel section. It has never moved from that spot, except when they dust with a squirrel hair brush. No one knows what a googly eye is for, exactly. It’s just nice to have someone watching the shelves.

The card catalog sits in the middle of the space, its drawers made from matchboxes, its labels written in Mabel’s tiny, looping script. Thistle, the calico cataloger with wire glasses made from a twist tie and broken watch crystal, is hunched over the top, copying titles from a new batch of mini books salvaged from a donated dollhouse last week. She’s hard of hearing—lost most of it to a bad cold last winter—reads lip movements when she can, relies on vibration through the oak shelves the rest of the time. The heating kicks on then, a low rattle that hums through the walls, shakes the matchbox drawers, drowns out all the small thumps and scratches Thistle uses to tell when someone’s approaching. Pip is walking past with a stack of fairy tale books, and without breaking stride, she taps Thistle’s shoulder twice, light as a dust mote, then keeps going. Thistle nods, doesn’t look up, just keeps writing. No “thanks,” no “you’re welcome,” no mention of it after.

When Thistle leans down to grab a catalog card from the bottom drawer, her shoulder brushes the back of the catalog frame, and a tiny scrap of paper flutters a little, peeking out from the crack. It’s a scrap of sheet music, so small you can only see two notes: G and B-flat. None of the librarians can read sheet music. They found it tucked in a mini piano instruction book in 2015, and tucked it behind the catalog because they liked the curve of the note heads. It’s been there ever since.

The return slot is cut into the bottom of the panel, just big enough for a mini book to fit through. Underneath it, a single matchbox drawer is labeled *ODD RETURNS* in Mabel’s script. Pip opens it to drop off a tiny book of sonnets someone left on the reading nook cushion, and you catch a glimpse of the contents: a tiny mother of pearl button, a scrap of tinfoil shaped like a tiny boat, and a single dried pea painted bright red with chipped pink nail polish. It showed up in the return slot in 1998, with a tiny slip of paper that just said sorry, wrong slot. No one knows who painted it, no one knows who returned it. It’s the first thing in the odd returns drawer, and it’s never been moved.

You drift toward the back of the space, where the roof pipe runs down the wall, and Fern slips in, shaking rain off her sleek black fur, her scarf—frayed from a 1960s cashmere sweater cuff—wrapped tight around her neck. She’s 45 minutes early for her night shift. She hangs her scarf on the hook by the wall calendar, which is printed on a sheet of 1980s mushroom postage stamps, and pauses. That morning, the calendar was turned to the sugar maple illustration, Mabel’s favorite. Now it’s on the chanterelle page, the one Fern always stops to stare at when she thinks no one’s looking. She blinks, twitches her whiskers, then pours herself a thimble of chamomile tea from the pot on the stove. No one mentions she’s early. No one mentions the calendar.

The reading nook is tucked in the far corner, under the rusty pipe that drips condensation into an acorn cap basin, drip drip drip mixing with the soft stir of the human librarian’s oat milk latte from the other side of the wall. There’s a cushion made from a velvet earring back, and a side table made from a soda bottle cap perched on a spool of thread. On the table, next to a half-open mini book of coastal lighthouses, sits a seashell the size of a pinhead, found in the book drop in 2021, left by a patron who’d just come back from Cannon Beach. None of the librarians have ever seen the ocean. They take turns holding it up to their ears sometimes when it’s rainy, even though they all know it doesn’t make any sound.

Right next to the nook, glued to the wall, is the smallest shelf in the entire collection: no bigger than a postage stamp, because it *is* a postage stamp, a 1912 one-cent Benjamin Franklin stamp, holding three mini books smaller than grains of rice, all about the history of United States postage stamps. No one has ever checked them out. No one has even opened them, as far as anyone knows. They just sit there, because the shelf is for stamp books, and the shelf is a stamp.

The rolling ladder leans against the history shelf now, and you glance at its rungs as you drift past. The third one from the bottom has a tiny dent in it. It got there in 2019, when a baby squirrel fell down the wall chimney and landed on the ladder before scurrying out the roof pipe. No one has ever bothered to bang the dent out, even though they have a tiny hammer made from a thumbtack in the tool drawer. No one even talks about the squirrel anymore. The dent is just part of the ladder.

Mabel opens her top desk drawer to grab a fresh darning needle, and you catch a glint of silver inside, tucked next to a pinhead-sized rubber eraser and a tiny length of thread: a single iridescent sequin from a 1920s flapper’s dress, found tucked in the spine of a 1923 mini edition of *The Waste Land* during a restoration project in 1998. It’s too scratchy to sew onto anything, too small to use as a paperweight. They just keep it there, because it catches the gray light just right.

By the time the hour is almost up, the rain has picked up a little, tapping harder on the skylight, and the light has faded to soft, dusky gray. Pip is curled up on the reading nook cushion, holding the tiny seashell up to her ear. Thistle is filing catalog cards, her tail flicking softly in time with the drip of the pipe. Fern is sipping her tea, staring at the chanterelle calendar page. Mabel is rearranging the new arrivals shelf, the daisy still tucked behind her apron string. The spider’s web sways a little from the draft of the heating vent, the shortbread crumb glinting in the gray light.

No one is in a hurry. No book is missing. No deadline is looming. It’s just a gray, drizzly mid-October Saturday, slow and soft, unfolding behind oak paneling, where the books are tiny and the librarians are smaller, and nothing much is happening, and that’s exactly the point.

dream_response:
The brass bell above the library’s front door jingles three times as the last patron—an 8-year-old with a neon green Goosebumps backpack slung over one shoulder—pulls the door shut behind him, his scuffed sneakers scuffing the sidewalk until the sound fades. That’s the start of the 17 minutes. The library smells like old paper, lemon Pledge, and the faint, sticky ghost of the bubblegum he was chewing under his hoodie.

The cranny fuzzles are already peeking out. They’re thumb-tall, with fur the color of dust that’s settled on hardcover spines for 20 years, pink paw pads the texture of eraser nubs, and tails tipped with smudges of blue and black ink from gnawing on pen caps left tucked in book gutters. They don’t have names, not really, just chirps that translate to things like glitter-paw, crumb-finder, button-tucker. The first one out squeezes through the gap between the checkout desk’s Formica top and its wooden side, right next to the faint sticky apple juice ring left by a dinosaur sippy cup last Tuesday. He taps the ring’s edge once with his left paw—sign-in ritual, no one remembers how it started, it’s just what you do. The rest follow, some of the younger glitter-paws tapping twice just to be silly, and the oldest fuzzle (the one with a scrap of 1989 library card stuck to her left ear) chirps soft, fake-scolding chirps that don’t mean anything at all.

Sitting half an inch from the juice ring is the rubber due-date stamp, its red rubber face missing the bottom left corner of its J, chipped when the head librarian dropped it on the linoleum in 1995. The glitter-paws line up at the edge of the stamp’s red ink pad for the nightly stamp hop: one by one, they leap onto the stamp’s face, land square in the missing J corner (their tiny, official stage), wiggle their whole fuzzy bodies in a bouncy little dance, then hop off onto the Formica, leaving pale pink paw prints that will dry completely by 8 a.m. They never step on the rest of the stamp—they know the librarians need it to work, and they don’t want to make trouble. The oldest fuzzle sits on the ink pad’s edge and counts them, chirping once for every dancer, just like she’s done every night since the J chipped.

From there, the group drifts toward the picture book nook, where the scratchy orange corduroy couch huddles against the wall under a window strung with construction paper turkeys from last month’s storytime. The left arm’s top button is loose, hanging by a single frayed white cotton thread. The button-tuckers—fuzzles with extra-fluffy paw pads, perfect for tucking thread—scramble up the couch’s wooden leg, pausing halfway to pluck orange fuzz out of their fur; the scratchy corduroy sheds like crazy, especially in October, and by the time they reach the arm they look like tiny, wobbly pumpkins. Each gives the button a gentle, tiny tug to check if the thread’s frayed more, then tucks the loose end back under the button’s edge as best they can with their little paws. When they’re done, each curls up in the shallow indent under the button for exactly three seconds, a tiny cozy power nap. The last tucker leaves a single scrap of *Where the Wild Things Are* page confetti (leftover from a 1993 mishap with a toddler and a pair of safety scissors) next to the button, as a thank-you for being a good nap spot.

Back by the reference section, the dented metal microfilm machine hums soft and off-key, a wobbly rendition of *At Last*—the head librarian listens to old jazz on her crackly transistor radio under the desk during lunch, and the machine absorbed the tunes, a tiny bit of semi-magic no human’s ever noticed. The dent on its top left corner (from a teen dropping a 1982 encyclopedia set on it in 1994) makes perfect footholds, and the hum-along crew climbs up to line along the machine’s warm top edge, chirping in time with the wobbly jazz. Some tap their paw pads against the dent, which makes a tiny, muffled thud that matches the rhythm, and the machine’s hum swells a little, like it’s happy to have an audience. This is the longest part of the routine; the metal stays warm from the day’s use, and the jazz is nice, so no one rushes.

Tucked behind the last reference shelf (the one with 1990 phone books stacked on the bottom) is the stack of 12 dog-eared *Baby-Sitters Club* paperbacks, their spines creased, their inside covers scribbled with crayon names and phone numbers that are half smudged. No one’s checked them out in exactly 3 years, 2 months, and 4 days—the fuzzles count, because they feel bad for the books, all lonely back there. After the hum-along, the page-tuckers work their way through the stack, flipping gently to the most dog-eared page of each: the margin of #12 where a kid drew a lopsided cat next to Claudia’s sketch of the new girl, the page in #4 where Mary Anne’s new haircut is described three times, the page in #8 where Kristy yells so loud the dialogue bubble takes up half the page. Into each fold they tuck a tiny, useless treasure: a silver glitter speck from last week’s craft, a crumb of pink eraser, a scrap of red ribbon from a bookmark left in a mystery novel, a tuft of orange corduroy fuzz. They don’t expect anything back. They just like giving the books little gifts, so they don’t feel forgotten. Tonight, the youngest glitter-paw tucks a crumb of lemon drop into the cat page of #12, and the page curls just a little, like it’s smiling.

The lemon drop crumb comes from the head librarian’s top desk drawer, which she always leaves slightly ajar—she fumbles with it when she reaches for her coffee mug and never remembers to push it all the way shut. Tucked in the back of the drawer is a glass jar with a red-and-white checkered lid, full of lemon drops, with fine yellow sugar crumbs caked along the rim. The head librarian thinks only she knows about those crumbs; she licks them off sometimes when she’s alone, and never mentions it to the other librarians because she thinks it’s silly. The fuzzles know about them too, but they only take the tiniest crumbs, the ones that are almost flaking off anyway, so she never notices. The oldest fuzzle—crumb-finder, too, these days—climbs the jar’s glass side every night, scrapes one tiny yellow crumb loose with her paw, and carries it carefully back to the reference shelf in her mouth. The whole group takes turns licking the tiniest speck of it, sour and sweet enough to make their whiskers tingle, and they always save the last bit for the BSC books.

At 16 minutes and 40 seconds, they hear the night librarian’s sneakers squeak on the break room linoleum—she always finishes her orange soda right on time, then comes out to lock up. No one rushes. They know the timing by heart. The hum-along crew chirps one last goodbye to the microfilm machine, which hums softer, like it’s saying goodnight back. The button-tuckers give the couch button one last pat. The glitter-paws give the stamp’s J corner one last wiggle. Every fuzzle taps the apple juice ring once on their way back to their crannies, sign-out ritual, same as always.

Exactly at 17 minutes, the night librarian flips the overhead light switch. The fluorescent bulbs flicker once, then go out, leaving only the tiny glow-in-the-dark star night-light by the children’s bathroom casting faint blue light over the picture books. She walks down the back hall, jiggles the storage closet handle to make sure it’s locked, then lets herself out the back door, the deadbolt clicking behind her.

The fuzzles are already tucked into their nests: some in the gap behind the checkout desk, lined with old checkout slips and orange corduroy fuzz; some in the couch’s spring box, curled up with lost puzzle pieces; some behind the microfilm machine, warm from the day’s heat; a few of the smallest ones curled in the folded pages of the BSC books, right next to the tiny treasures. They’re sleepy, their whiskers still tingling from lemon drop, and they don’t have anything to do tomorrow except watch people read and do the whole 17 minutes all over again. It’s perfect.

dream_response:
The humidity sticks to the back of your neck like a half-peeled sticker, thin and warm, when you push through the community garden’s rusted wire gate at 7:12pm—no reason to be there other than your sneakers turned left instead of right at the end of the driveway. The sun’s softened to something that doesn’t burn, just gilds the edges of everything, and the first raised bed you pass has chipped tangerine paint flaking along its top rail, pale as dried citrus peel, worn down from years of people resting their knees while weeding.

Your cotton sleeve catches on a tomato cage as you veer around lopsided volunteer marigolds, and the sharp, grassy-green scent of tomato leaves bursts up, bright enough to make you blink, a tiny unripe green fruit bumping your wrist cool as a marble. A puff of dandelion seeds lifts from a crack in the dirt path when your sandal scuffs the edge, each one glowing pale honey-gold for half a beat before settling in the grass between the beds, faint as embers that don’t catch. You don’t pause; you’ve seen it a hundred times, same as the dandelions by the library sidewalk that do the same after rain.

Somewhere three houses over, a glass lemonade pitcher clinks against a ceramic rim, the sound thin and bright through oak boughs, tangled up with the low drone of a window unit humming through a screen. You drift toward the back of the garden where the mint bed runs along the split-rail fence, and when the wind shifts, it doesn’t smell like summer mint—like mojitos or iced tea—but like the peppermint candy canes you stashed in your winter coat pocket last December, sweet and sharp and cold, even with the air thick enough to sip. You pluck a leaf, roll it between thumb and forefinger, and the candy cane scent sticks to your skin like lip balm.

The sunflower row is next, stalks taller than your shoulder, heads heavy with soft, pale milky seeds. You squint at a stalk where a ladybug trundles up, slow as a tourist, leaving a faint iridescent trail pearlescent as the inside of a seashell, only visible if you tilt your head just right so the golden sun hits it. It fades after a minute, same as all the others, no trace left but the ladybug, vanished somewhere in the sunflower’s fuzzy yellow petals.

Your calves ache a little, so you sink onto the edge of a bare dirt patch by the clover that grows where the last raised bed rotted out three years ago. You lean forward, ear an inch from the leaves, and there it is: the hum, soft as a lullaby played on a toy piano, coming from every fourth clover leaf, thrumming so quiet you can barely feel it through the air. You stay there for a minute, counting hums in time with distant cicada buzz, until a gnat buzzes past your ear and you sit back, brushing dirt crumbs off your denim shorts.

When you stand, your knees creak, and you glance at your watch—7:19, only seven minutes passed, feels like longer. You turn left toward the wild blackberry brambles along the back fence, no particular destination, candy cane mint scent still on your fingers, clover hum still faint in the back of your ears. A dandelion seed lands on your wrist, glows gold for half a second, then sticks to the sweat there, light as a breath.

dream_response:
You find the nook by accident, when you’re yanking on the stuck third drawer of the dented metal microfilm cabinet, the one that holds all the 1982 issues of the *Maplewood Gazette*, the paper with the weekly cat photo column on the back page. The drawer gives with a lurch, and the cabinet shifts sideways just enough to reveal a gap between its back and the cinder block wall, just wide enough to squeeze through if you hold your breath and turn sideways, your shoulder brushing the frayed edge of a stack of 1988 *National Geographics* tucked against the wall.

The other side is smaller than you expect, a cranny tucked under a smudged casement window streaked with the rainbow residue of a 1994 summer reading craft where kids glued tissue paper squares to glass. A neon green T-Rex sticker, peeling at the corners, is stuck to the lower pane—you remember getting one just like it from the grocery store vending machine for a quarter last year. Sun slants through in thick, dust-mottled bars, gilding the edges of a wobbly pine side table propped up on its back left leg with a water-damaged 1982 *Guinness Book of World Records* (the one with the world’s longest fingernails on the cover, the photo that made you cringe when you were seven).

Draped over the table’s edge, half pooling on the scuffed linoleum, is a frayed knit throw: 100% 1980s Red Heart acrylic, scratchy-smooth under your fingertips, pilled into tiny tight nubs along every rib stitch, its edges frayed so bad the loose threads curl like pale yellow caterpillars, soft at the very tips from being tugged a thousand times but still rough enough to leave a faint pink line if you rub your wrist against it too fast. The corner that’s been tucked under the table’s wobbly leg to prop it up is stiff with a faint brown ring of old hot cocoa that never quite wiped clean, and if you sniff it, it smells like cinnamon and old library dust and just a hint of the cherry Kool-Aid someone spilled on it in 1991.

Tucked against the cinder block wall is a lumpy brown corduroy armchair, its left arm torn open along the seam and held together with three strips of clear packing tape that have yellowed at the edges. The cushion sinks so far down when you sit that your knees are almost level with your chest, and the corduroy is worn smooth along the armrests where hundreds of people have rested their elbows. As soon as your weight settles, a hard candy materializes on the chipped white windowsill, right where the sun hits it. It’s round, translucent, the color of weak sun tea, with a tiny fleck of something green suspended dead center, like a bug that got stuck in amber but smaller, softer. You pop it in your mouth, and the first flavor is sweet, like the melted vanilla ice cream that drips down the side of a waffle cone at a Fourth of July parade, the kind that gets sticky on your wrist and you lick off later when no one’s looking. Then it fades into a faint, briny-sour zing of dill pickle, not enough to be weird, just enough to make you blink, like the candy remembered a church potluck it went to once and forgot to leave the pickle jar off the dessert table.

It takes you a minute to notice the tiny figures moving around on the windowsill, half-hidden behind a stack of old due date slips tied with frayed red string. The first one you spot is a hedgehog, no bigger than your thumbnail, with quills that look like tiny brown toothpicks and a little knitted scarf around his neck that’s slightly too big. He’s sitting on a 1978 penny, cross-legged (as cross-legged as a hedgehog can be), and he’s complaining to a mouse in a tiny tweed jacket who’s sorting through a pile of sequins. You lean in a little, and his voice is high and squeaky, like a wind-up toy that’s almost run out of batteries.

“And don’t even get me started on that new self-checkout machine by the front door,” he huffs, poking a silver sequin with his paw so hard it skitters across the windowsill and lands in a crack in the wood. “Beeps so loud it makes my quills tingle for ten whole minutes after. Last Tuesday some kid scanned twelve Berenstain Bears books in a row right by the microfilm cabinet, and I had to hide in a pencil cup under the reference desk until the tingling stopped. Embarrassing, is what it is. A hedgehog of my standing—third from the left in the *Hedgehog Harvest Festival* feast spread, got the single line about passing the berry tarts—hiding in a pencil cup with a bunch of broken crayons.”

He picks up a pine needle from a little pile next to him, picks at a nonexistent crumb between his teeth, and huffs again. “Another thing? The kid who used to check out my book every October? Always left a cherry lollipop stick between pages 14 and 15, right by my spot. Used to be my favorite thing, licking the leftover sticky off when the book was on the hold shelf. But now they moved the book to back storage, no one checks it out anymore, and the windowsill candy never has cherry. It’s always vanilla-pickle or maple-sage or some other nonsense. No respect for tradition, that’s what.”

He jabs the pine needle at the mouse in the tweed jacket, who doesn’t even look up from sorting sequins. “And you! You keep stealing my pine needle toothpicks! I curate those, you know. I get ’em off the Christmas wreath the library puts up every December, the good ones, the ones that are stiff and don’t break when you’re picking blackberry seeds out of your teeth. There are perfectly good pine needles by the fern by the front door, but no, you have to take mine. Just to be annoying, I swear.” The mouse just twitches his whiskers and tucks the pine needle into the breast pocket of his tweed jacket, which makes the hedgehog huff so hard his scarf slips off one shoulder.

A little girl no bigger than your thumbnail is sitting on the edge of the wobbly side table, swinging her legs, wearing red polka dot rain boots that are slightly too big for her and a yellow raincoat with a hood that’s flopped down over her shoulders. She’s twisting a dandelion fluff between her fingers, and she’s smiling so wide her cheeks are pink. You hear her murmur something to the mouse, who nods, and she holds up the dandelion like it’s a trophy.

“Mabel curled up on my book box for three afternoons in a row this week,” she says, and her voice sounds like wind chimes made out of tiny glass beads. “The tabby cat who sleeps on the hold shelf? She’s got a little white patch on her chest that looks like a lopsided heart. The warmth seeped right through the cardboard and the book pages, and I got to nap in sun-warmed paper that smelled like cat fur and library dust. It was the coziest I’ve been since 1992, when the kid who checked out *Maggie’s Mud Pie Adventure* brought me to a blanket fort in their backyard and left me in a patch of sun for an hour. I’m only on page 27, just wave at Maggie from the sidewalk, no lines—so I don’t get out much. I even found a piece of cat fur stuck to the edge of my page this morning. I’m keeping it in my rain boot. Right next to the tiny piece of pink sidewalk chalk I found last month.”

For a minute, no one says anything, and you can hear the hum of the library’s clunky old HVAC unit, low and rumbly, like a giant’s purr. It’s a B-flat, you think, the kind that vibrates in your back teeth if you’re too close to the vent by the reference desk, but back here it’s softened by all the stacked book boxes and the frayed knit throw, so it just settles in your bones, warm and steady. Every 47 seconds, it hiccups a little click, when the fan shifts speed to circulate more air. Mixed right in with the hum is the noise of the craft project they’re all working on: tiny, precise snips from a pair of scissors half the size of a thumbtack (stolen from the front desk’s pencil cup, the pair with the pink plastic handles that have a unicorn sticker on them), the soft squish of a glue stick that’s almost dried out, so it makes a little tacky sound every time someone presses it to paper, and the faint, tinny clink of a sequin being dropped into a mason jar lid full of other sequins—gold, silver, neon pink, the kind left over from summer reading crafts. The sounds are timed just off-beat with the HVAC’s clicks—every time the unit rumbles its little hiccup, the scissors snip half a second later, like they’re having a quiet, slow conversation no one else is invited to. The spider who lives in the top corner of the nook (she’s got a tiny red stripe on her back, and she was the background spider on page 19 of *Ben’s Backyard Bug Hunt*, 1987) is stringing the finished bunting triangles—cut from old overdue notice slips, edged with sequins—along her web, and the silk hums a little too, high and thin, right above the HVAC’s low rumble.

You lose track of time for a while, just watching the sequins glint and the dandelion seeds float in the sunbeams. The ice cream truck jingle drifts through the cracked window, loud at first, then fainter, until it’s just a memory of a tune. A ladybug crawls across the windowsill, and the little girl in the rain boots gasps and leans in so far she almost falls off the table edge. The hedgehog curls up on his penny, his scarf pulled up over his nose, and falls asleep, snoring so softly it sounds like the rustle of a page turning. The mouse keeps sorting sequins, tucking the shiniest gold ones into his tweed pocket for later. The spider keeps stringing bunting, her tiny legs moving so fast they’re a blur.

At one point, you reach out and touch the knit throw again, running your finger along the frayed edges, and one of the loose yellow threads comes off in your hand. You tuck it into the pocket of your jeans, just a little souvenir. The candy on your tongue is almost gone, just a faint hint of pickle and vanilla left at the back of your throat. A dust mote floats through the sunbeam, slow as a boat, and you watch it drift all the way from the window to the top of the *Guinness Book* under the table leg.

When the sun has moved just far enough that the golden bar that was on the table edge is now hitting the top of the stack of 1996 *Weekly Reader*s on the floor—you count, that’s 25 minutes, almost exactly, because you know how fast the sun moves through this library’s windows, you’ve spent enough afternoons here reading under the front windows—you hear a faint clatter from the microfilm cabinet outside the nook, like someone’s trying to pull open a drawer.

The little girl in the rain boots waves at you, quick, like she’s not supposed to be seen by anyone else. The mouse twitches his whiskers in a little salute. The hedgehog snores on, oblivious.

You squeeze back through the gap between the microfilm cabinet and the wall, and when you turn around, the gap is gone, like it was never there. The microfilm drawer is still stuck, just like it was before. You reach into your pocket, and the loose yellow thread from the knit throw is still there, soft at the tip, a little scratchy.

No one asks you where you were. No one even notices you were gone. The library hums on, same as always.
